subject: social
source: NCERT Democratic Politics II (Class X Political Science), Chapter 4

topics.name: Why do we need political parties?
How many parties should we have?

questions.q: A group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government is called a…
questions.e: They agree on policies and programmes to promote the collective good.

questions.q: What are the three components of a political party?
questions.a: The leaders, the active members and the followers
w: The President, Prime Minister and Speaker
questions.e: Parties are about a part of society and involve partisanship.

questions.q: A person strongly committed to a party, group or faction, unable to take a balanced view, is…
questions.e: Partisanship is a tendency to take a side.

questions.q: In India, who usually chooses a party’s candidates for elections?
w: All members and supporters of the party
questions.e: In the USA, members and supporters choose candidates.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of political parties?
questions.a: Acting as an umpire in disputes between levels of government
w: Providing access to government machinery and welfare schemes
questions.e: That is the job of the courts.

questions.q: Why are political parties necessary for democracy?
questions.a: Without parties every candidate would be independent, no one could promise major policy changes and no one would be responsible for running the country
w: Parties are needed to appoint judges
Parties keep the army in check
questions.e: The rise of parties is linked to representative democracy.

questions.q: Which statements about parties are correct? A. Parties do not enjoy much trust among people  B. Parties are often rocked by scandals involving top leaders  C. Parties are not necessary to run governments
questions.e: C is wrong – parties are necessary (NCERT exercise 10).

Deciding how members vote on a Bill in the legislature
Recruiting and training leaders to become ministers
Criticising the government for wrong policies
Helping a citizen approach a welfare scheme
questions.e: {x} → {ans}.

questions.q: In China only the Communist Party is allowed to rule. This is a…
questions.e: It is not a democratic option – democracy needs at least two competing parties.

questions.q: The USA and the United Kingdom are examples of a…
questions.e: Power usually changes between two main parties.

questions.q: India has a…
questions.e: Several parties have a reasonable chance of coming to power, alone or in alliance.

questions.q: About how many parties are registered with the Election Commission of India?
questions.e: But only a handful are serious contenders.

questions.q: When several parties in a multiparty system join hands to contest elections and win power, it is called…
questions.e: In 2004: NDA, UPA and Left Front.

questions.q: Why has India evolved a multiparty system?
questions.a: The social and geographical diversity of such a large country is not easily absorbed by two or three parties
w: The Constitution fixes the number of parties
The Election Commission prefers many parties
Two parties are illegal in India
questions.e: A party system evolves over time; it cannot be chosen.

questions.q: According to the surveys in the chapter, which is true for India?
questions.a: Trust in parties is low but participation in party activities is fairly high and rising
w: Indians are less likely to be party members than Canadians
questions.e: Membership in India is higher than in Canada, Japan, Spain and South Korea.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A one-party system is not a good option.
Reason (R): It is not a democratic option because voters do not get a free choice.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.e: Any democratic system must allow at least two parties to compete fairly.

questions.q: Who founded the Bahujan Samaj Party?
questions.e: Formed in 1984 to represent the bahujan samaj – dalits, adivasis, OBCs and religious minorities.

questions.q: What is the guiding philosophy of the Bharatiya Janata Party?
questions.e: Also Antyodaya; cultural nationalism (Hindutva) is important to its idea of the nation.

questions.q: The Indian National Congress was founded in…
questions.e: One of the oldest parties of the world.

questions.q: How many recognised national parties were there as per the Election Commission’s 2023 notification?
questions.e: AAP, BJP, BSP, CPI(M), INC and NPP.

questions.q: According to the chapter, a party is recognised as a State party if it secures at least … of votes in a State assembly election and wins at least … seats.
questions.e: National party: 6% votes in Lok Sabha or assembly elections in four States and at least four Lok Sabha seats.

questions.q: Which was the first party from North-East India to attain national party status?
questions.e: Formed in July 2013 under P.A. Sangma; formed the government in Meghalaya.

questions.q: Which party was in power in West Bengal without a break for 34 years?
questions.e: Founded in 1964; believes in Marxism-Leninism; strong in West Bengal, Kerala and Tripura.

questions.q: Since 1996, the participation of State parties in national coalition governments has…
questions.e: Nearly every State party has been part of a national-level coalition.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four challenges to political parties described in the chapter?
questions.a: Too many elections held by the Election Commission
w: Growing role of money and muscle power
questions.e: The fourth challenge is the lack of a meaningful choice for voters.

questions.q: Changing party allegiance from the party on which a person got elected to a different party is called…
questions.e: The Constitution was amended so that a defecting MLA or MP loses the seat.

questions.q: After a Supreme Court order, every candidate must file an affidavit giving details of…
questions.a: property and criminal cases pending against them
questions.e: This made information public, but there is no system to check if it is true.

questions.q: What was a side-effect of the anti-defection law?
questions.a: It made any dissent more difficult – MPs and MLAs must accept what party leaders decide
w: It gave women one-third of tickets
questions.e: It brought defection down but strengthened party bosses.

questions.q: Which suggestion has been made but NOT yet accepted by parties?
w: Organisational elections ordered by the Election Commission
questions.e: Other suggestions: a law on internal affairs and one-third tickets for women.

questions.q: Why must we be careful about legal solutions to party reform?
questions.a: Over-regulation can be counter-productive and push parties to find ways to cheat the law
questions.e: People’s pressure and more people joining parties are other ways to reform.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Dynastic succession is a challenge to political parties.
Reason (R): Most parties do not practise open and transparent procedures, so ordinary workers find it hard to rise to the top.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.e: The lack of transparency (R) is why family members get unfair advantage (A).

questions.q: A party wins 7% of votes in a State Assembly election and 3 seats. What is its status?
questions.a: It is recognised as a State party
w: It must merge with a national party
questions.e: State party: at least 6% of votes and at least 2 seats in a State Assembly election.
questions.passage: Every party in the country has to register with the Election Commission. While the Commission treats all parties equally, it offers some special facilities to large and established parties. These parties are given a unique symbol – only the official candidates of that party can use that election symbol. A party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in an election to the Legislative Assembly of a State and wins at least two seats is recognised as a State party. A party that secures at least six per cent of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or Assembly elections in four States and wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha is recognised as a national party.

questions.q: What special facility does the Election Commission give to recognised parties?
questions.a: A unique election symbol that only its official candidates can use
questions.e: The symbol is the key facility mentioned in the passage.

questions.q: To be a national party, a party must win at least how many Lok Sabha seats (with 6% votes)?
questions.e: 6% votes in Lok Sabha or in Assembly elections in four States + at least 4 Lok Sabha seats.
